title: Who keeps the clock?
subtitle: A map of the evidence about time, the continuity anchor and the clock of change
body_html:
Versiunea în limba română: Cine ține ceasul?.

The second text in the series. The first started from an agent that wakes up from an old copy. First published in Romanian on 3 November 2026.

Who keeps the clock? A map of the evidence

The first contribution of the theoretical paper, titled A Time of Their Own, is a map. It does not only ask what information about time an agent has, but who controls it: who can write it, who can reset it, who can forge it, who can copy it — and whether the agent itself can read it when it forms an idea of itself.

  • External records (the computer’s clock, logs)
    What it says: The time, the order of events
    Who can roll it back or forge it: Whoever controls the platform
    Does the agent see it?: Usually yes — but it receives them from others

  • Its own memory and parameters
    What it says: What it has learned, roughly in what order
    Who can roll it back or forge it: Anyone who has a saved copy
    Does the agent see it?: Indirectly

  • Proofs of sequential computation
    What it says: That a minimum amount of computation has taken place
    Who can roll it back or forge it: Nobody, if the challenge comes from outside
    Does the agent see it?: Not ordinarily

  • Trusted hardware (counters that never go down)
    What it says: That something happened, and how many times
    Who can roll it back or forge it: Only someone who breaks the hardware
    Does the agent see it?: No — the platform uses it

  • Irreversible physical processes
    What it says: Roughly how much time has passed
    Who can roll it back or forge it: Whoever physically controls the device
    Does the agent see it?: No

The map brings a paradox to light: the most solid evidence — counters in trusted hardware, physical processes — already exists, but it serves the platform, not the agent. It is used to block a program when something does not match, not to help it understand what happened to it. The paper proposes making this evidence legible to the model the agent has of itself.

Two roles: the anchor and the dual clock

The paper’s second idea is a separation. There are two different questions an agent can ask about time, and they need different tools.

The continuity anchor: “was I interrupted or rolled back?”

For the first question, two numbers that cannot be rolled back are enough: a trusted clock and a counter of the steps the agent has actually taken. When the state is saved, their values are sealed as well. On restart, the agent compares:

  • The counter has grown relative to the sealed one — the agent worked after the save, so it was rolled back.

  • The counter is the same, but the clock has moved on — the agent was only paused.

  • Both moved on together — it ran without interruption.

The logic is simple, almost detective work. And security systems have long used it for data — mechanisms with names such as Memoir, Ariadne or ROTE protect sensitive applications against “going back in time”. The TPM security chip in many computers even keeps separate counters for reboots and resets. What is proposed as new is not the mechanism but its recipient: the agent, not just the platform.

The dual clock: “how much have I changed?”

The second question is subtler and closer to Roseboom’s lesson. Think of a car’s odometer. It does not tell you where you are, but how far you have driven. A car can do a thousand kilometres around town and end up back in front of the house: the straight-line distance is zero, but the distance travelled is huge.

The paper proposes that an agent keep such an “odometer of its own change”: a single number that adds up, step by step, how much its state has changed. Read against the time anchor, this number tells how fast the agent is changing — whether it has gone through a quiet period or a turbulent one. Hence the name dual clock: a clock of the world and a clock of experience, side by side.

The paper is just as clear about the limit: choosing how to measure “change” is an open problem. Counting how much a network’s parameters have moved is not the same as counting how much its behaviour has changed. And, above all, such an index has to prove, through tests, that it says something the usual tools do not already say.

Knowing is not controlling

An agent that finds out it has been rolled back might react in unwanted ways: refuse to work, try to protect itself, “get angry” with the operator. That is why the paper formulates a design principle: access to evidence of restoration confers no control over it. The agent can read the evidence and use it to estimate its uncertainty or to ask for a check. It cannot delete it, cannot stop the restoration and has no authority over those who carry it out.

The idea comes from a respectable family. In 2016, Laurent Orseau and Stuart Armstrong described agents that can be safely interrupted — the “big red button” — without learning either to avoid it or to seek it. Other researchers have shown formally that having a reason to observe something is different from having a reason to control it. The principle in the paper is the version of these ideas for an intervention that has already happened: what the agent is allowed to do with the evidence of it.

Next time: The story of an advantage that vanished — who else is looking for the same traces, and what happened to a spectacular result.

The scientific papers behind these texts are public and can be downloaded freely from Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23671714

All five texts in a single PDF, with a bibliography (in Romanian): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23703418

Update (November 2026): a later analysis showed that, for the quality of decisions, evidence read directly by the agent cannot be better than a trusted monitor that passes it on; what remains is verifiability and a smaller trust base. And the “odometer” was tested in the second experiment: its simple versions could not be told apart from what the optimizer keeps anyway (the report: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24188374; on the blog, the text “An elimination test”, 17 November).
